effect_estimate.comment: No multivariable regression or inferential statistical test is conducted; the paper reports primary descriptive census statistics on privatization and market concentration alongside narrative synthesis of prior Spanish studies and descriptive national administrative statistics on network leakage and drinking-water quality reporting compliance.
effect_estimate.value: Descriptive legal-institutional and census findings (no inferential numeric effect estimate reported): legally regulated private management supplies urban water in 23% of Spanish municipalities covering 55% of the population (operating in municipalities averaging 14,008 inhabitants vs. 3,416 inhabitants under public management), with two dominant companies (AGBAR and Aqualia) managing 67% of privatized municipalities and 75% of the privatized population, and 18 of 37 available 2013-2014 public tenders attracting either 0 bidders (5 cases) or 1 bidder (13 cases). Prior Spanish empirical studies reviewed in Section 3 show no conclusive efficiency advantage of private over public management once environmental factors are controlled, mixed/context-dependent higher residential water prices under contracting-out/privatization, and higher unaccounted-for water under public-private partnerships in Southern Spain. Under Spain's fragmented municipal model and regulatory/oversight deficit, unaccounted-for water averages 25% nationally and frequently exceeds 60% in small municipalities, while in 2011 SINAC received no drinking-water quality information for 10.2% of the population and only 37% of municipalities (42% of the population) reported mandatory consumer-tap water quality analyses (leaving 58% of the population without reported tap-water quality data).

mechanism_certainty.comment: Appraised under the Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework (design ceiling = 2). Coded as 1 (documented descriptive/statistical association) because the authors document descriptive municipal census patterns, secondary econometric literature on prices/leakage, and aggregate administrative statistics on network losses and SINAC water-quality reporting non-compliance linked to municipal fragmentation and regulatory deficits, rather than directly observing household-level service outcomes produced by an administrative mechanism in primary fieldwork.

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines municipal atomization across 8,117 local governments and multi-tier administrative dispersion (institutional_fragmentation), weak inter-municipal cooperation and vertical coordination across administrative levels (political_coordination), concession charges passed onto residential water tariffs and unregulated municipal tariff variation (fees), wide municipal discretion and local regulatory capture in contract and tariff oversight (discretion), weak enforcement and failure to impose statutory penalties under Royal Decree 140/2003 and EU wastewater rules (sanction), and contractual opacity and weak citizen participation in urban water governance (participation).

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: The paper is a legal-institutional and regulatory analysis of Spain's municipal water governance model supported by primary descriptive municipal census fieldwork (privatization shares, market concentration, tender bidder counts, and review of tariff revision proceedings), secondary administrative data (SINAC, INE, MHAP), and a narrative review of Spanish empirical studies. Because it contains primary empirical institutional/legal data rather than being a pure essay, and fits none of the six conventional epidemiological/social-science study designs (no analytical cross-sectional exposure-outcome regression, quasi-experiment, qualitative interview protocol, or systematic review search), the Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework applies.

sample_size.comment: Spain has 8,117 municipalities, and the authors report percentages of Spanish municipalities and population from census fieldwork undertaken for their research (mapped across Spain in Fig. 1), though they do not state whether any municipalities had missing data. Footnote 9 additionally reports bidder counts for 37 municipal water-service tender processes in 2013-2014 (5 + 13 + 3 + 9 + 5 + 1 + 1 = 37 cases), and Section 5.4 reports 2011 SINAC national administrative records across Spanish municipalities.

study_design.comment: Combines primary descriptive census fieldwork mapping private vs. public municipal water management and market concentration across Spain with a narrative review of Spanish public-vs-private performance studies, secondary administrative statistics (SINAC, INE, MHAP), and critical legal-institutional analysis of municipal concession tendering, regulatory deficits, and administrative fragmentation.
study_design.value: Legal-institutional and policy analysis combined with descriptive national municipal census fieldwork, secondary administrative data analysis, and narrative literature review
